facts.subject: Well at the World's End
facts.statement: By the book, the woman drank of the Well, thrives ever after and lives yet.

refs.q: found it at the long last, and drank thereof, and throve ever after

facts.subject: (unnamed) woman of the book
facts.statement: By the book, she now serves the Well, keeping seekers from drinking by binding them in love.

refs.q: is become the servant of the Well to entangle the seekers in her love and keep them from drinking thereof

facts.subject: (unnamed) book of the Well
facts.statement: The book is fairly written with many pictures, including the image of the woman Ralph freed.

refs.q: amongst them was the image of the fair woman whom he had holpen at the want-ways of the wood

events.label: Tale of the woman of the book
events.summary: Wildwood maiden wed by a king's son, war over her, thraldom to a sorceress, rescue by a Well-seeker, escape from robbers, drinking of the Well.

refs.q: whereof befel long and grievous war which she abode not to the end

unresolved.question: Whether the book's woman is the Lady of Abundance and the lady of the crossroads; Ralph assumes so but does not know.

refs.q: Though he knew not for certain whether this tale had to do with the Lady of the Forest

unresolved.question: Ralph met the lady four days before.

refs.q: but four days ago was that

opportunities.idea: Legends in books that may be partial or slanted; the player can compare written lore with witnesses.

basis_refs.q: The book told not much about the Well at the World's End

ledger.summary: Ralph reads the book all night. Among its pictures is the woman he rescued. The book tells of a woman no man can help loving: found in the wildwood by a king's son, wed, his kingdom lost and long war over her; she returns to the wildwood, becomes thrall to a sorceress, is carried off by a Well-seeking knight who is slain, escapes robbers who fight over her, finds the Well and drinks, lives on and now serves the Well by ensnaring seekers in love so they never drink. Ralph is lovesick.
ledger.geography_notes: none; the Well story places the woman's old dwelling in the wildwood.
open_questions: Is the book's woman the lady of the crossroads and the Lady of Abundance?
